# Introduction \label{Introduction}

This report will look at how offshore economic and policy uncertainty affects the local equity market, and whether local funds need more protection against volatility. Part A will establish whether local volatility has increased and whether it follows global markets. Part B will evaluate whether SafeCore has navigated volatility effectively, where its volatility comes from and what its factor exposures are. Part C will look at the alpha opportunity in the local market since 2020 and how it changes with global policy uncertainty.

# Part A: \label{PartA}

## Data and approach

This section will look at whether volatility on the local stock exchange has increased and whether it follows global markets. Volatility refers to how much returns of an asset deviates from its average and is measured as the standard deviation (of daily returns). It is annualised by multiplying it by the square root of 252, which is the approximate number of trading days in a year, so that the figures are easier to compare.

The local market is represented by the Capped SWIX (J433), which is the broad market index and the fund's benchmark, together with the Mid Cap (J201) and Small Cap (J202) indexes. Including the size indexes shows whether changes in volatility are limited to the largest companies or are present across the market. Global markets are represented by MSCI World, which covers developed markets, and MSCI Emerging Markets (South Africa is typically grouped with other emerging markets by global investors). The comparison starts in 2015 as this is the first date of the local data. The MSCI indexes are in USD and the local indexes in ZAR, so naturally part of any difference in levels is due to currency movements.

```{r PartA_Rets}
# Local equity: Capped SWIX (J433, the fund benchmark), Mid Caps (J201) and
# Small Caps (J202), which are more domestically driven than the large caps
Local_Rets <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"))

# Global equity: MSCI World (developed markets) and MSCI EM (emerging market peers),
# converted from levels to daily returns, from 2015 (start of the local data)
Global_Rets <-
  MSCI %>%
  filter(Ticker %in% c("MXWO Index", "MXEF Index")) %>%
  Q1_Level_to_Returns() %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20150101))

# Stack local and global returns into one data frame
Eq_Rets <- bind_rows(Local_Rets, Global_Rets)
```

## Volatility over time

The first measure is a rolling standard deviation. For each day, the standard deviation is calculated over the previous 63 trading days and the window then moves forward one day at a time. A 63 day window (roughly three months) was chosen as it reacts to changes in the market without being too noisy. It also matches the three month horizon of the SAVIUSD currency volatility index.

```{r Figure_RollVol, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling 3 month annualised volatility: local vs global equity \\label{Figure_RollVol}", fig.height = 5, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
Roll_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>% Q1_Rolling_Vol(Window = 63)

g_roll <- Roll_Vol %>%
  mutate(Region = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"), "Local", "Global")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollSD, color = Name), alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Region, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Rolling Volatility: Local vs Global Equity",
     subtitle = "63 day rolling standard deviation, annualised",
     x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_roll, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_RollVol} shows that local and global volatility both have the largest increases happening at the same time, thus they tend to move closely together. In 2020 and in 2025, local and global volatility increased together (and by a similar amount). This suggests that local markets are affected by shocks that start offshore. In the most recent period, local volatility has increased together with emerging market volatility and developed market volatility has stayed low.

## Has volatility increased?

As the rolling measure can be difficult to read over a long period, Figure \ref{Figure_AnnVol} summarises volatility by calendar year instead.

```{r Figure_AnnVol, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Calendar year realised volatility \\label{Figure_AnnVol}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# Realised volatility per calendar year which is SD of daily returns within each year (annualised with sqrt(252))
Annual_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  group_by(Name, Year) %>%
  summarise(SD = sd(Returns, na.rm = T) * sqrt(252)) %>% ungroup()

g_ann <- Annual_Vol %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Year, SD, fill = Name), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Realised Volatility by Calendar Year", subtitle = "Standard deviation of daily returns, annualised (2016 to September 2026)", x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_ann, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1, x.vert = T)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_AnnVol} shows that local volatility has not increased steadily over time. Instead, it increases in ceratin episodes. There are clear peaks in 2020, 2022 and 2026. Apart from 2020, Capped SWIX volatility in 2026 is the highest since 2015, although the 2026 figure only includes data up to September. Mid and small cap volatility has stayed above its pre-2020 level since 2021, which suggests that the increase is not limited to the largest companies. Local volatility is also higher than MSCI World in almost every year and closer to MSCI Emerging Markets. In 2026, volatility rose again across all of the series considered. The increase was most pronounced for emerging markets, while developed market volatility rose by less. Local volatility followed this increase, although to a lesser extent than emerging markets as a group.

## Separating the volatility signal from noise

A limitation of the rolling standard deviation is that it is noisy, as a single extreme day affects the estimate for the whole window. A GARCH model addresses this by separating returns into an underlying level of volatility, called sigma, and random day-to-day noise. It does this by using the fact that volatility tends to cluster, meaning that a volatile day is usually followed by another volatile day.

This section uses a GJR-GARCH model, which allows negative returns to increase volatility by more than positive returns of the same size (the leverage effect). This was chosen as the standard GARCH model treats positive and negative shocks the same, while in practice negative returns in stock markets tend to raise volatility by more than positive returns. The model is fitted to the Capped SWIX and MSCI World separately.

```{r PartA_Garch, cache = TRUE}
# Fit the GJR-GARCH model to the Capped SWIX and MSCI World separately (one list element per ticker)
Garch_Out <-
  Eq_Rets %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "MXWO Index")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  group_split(Tickers) %>%
  map(~Q1_Garch_Sigma(.))
```

```{r Figure_Garch, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "GJR-GARCH conditional volatility: Capped SWIX vs MSCI World \\label{Figure_Garch}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# Stack the sigma series of both tickers and plot them together
g_garch <-
  Garch_Out %>% map_df(~.$Sigma) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, sigma, color = Tickers), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "GJR-GARCH Conditional Volatility", subtitle = "Capped SWIX vs MSCI World (Annualised Sigma)", x = "Year", y = "Annualised sigma") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_garch, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_Garch} shows that the large increases in global volatility, such as in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2025, line up with increases in local volatility. This suggests that local markets follow global markets during periods of stress. Global volatility increases more sharply during these episodes. In calmer periods local volatility remains higher than that of developed markets. The 2026 increase is different, as local volatility rose while developed market volatility stayed low. This matches the emerging market pattern in Figures \ref{Figure_RollVol} and \ref{Figure_AnnVol}.

```{r Table_Garch, results = 'asis'}
# Full GJR-GARCH coefficient tables (estimates, standard errors and p-values)
Table <- xtable(Garch_Out[[1]]$Coefs, caption = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) estimates: Capped SWIX \\label{Table_Garch_J433}", digits = 4)
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')

Table <- xtable(Garch_Out[[2]]$Coefs, caption = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) estimates: MSCI World \\label{Table_Garch_MXWO}", digits = 4)
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')
```

Tables \ref{Table_Garch_J433} and \ref{Table_Garch_MXWO} report the estimated parameters of the model. The parameter alpha1 measures how much volatility reacts to any new shock, gamma1 measures the extra reaction to negative shocks, and beta1 measures how much of yesterday’s volatility carries over to today. Persistence combines these and shows how slowly a volatility shock fades, where values close to one mean that shocks fade slowly.

For both indexes, alpha1 is close to zero while gamma1 is large, although the p-values of a GARCH fit should not be interpreted too strictly. Therefore, volatility increases mainly after negative returns rather than after positive ones. This effect is stronger for MSCI World, which is consistent with the sharper global spikes in Figure \ref{Figure_Garch}. Persistence is close to one for both indexes, at 0.968 for the Capped SWIX and 0.981 for MSCI World, so once volatility increases in either market it takes a long time to settle.

## Summary

In summary, local volatility has not increased steadily. It does seem to increase sharply when offshore shocks hit, and these shocks are then passed on to the local market. The most recent rise in volatility in 2026 was broad-based, but was strongest in emerging markets. This means that local funds remain exposed to offshore uncertainty.

# Part B: 

This section will look at whether SafeCore has handled volatility well. As volatility is not explicitly considered when SafeCore is constructed, its lack of a low volatility tilt is not surprising. However, the results show that the fund does not avoid volatility by chance either. It is concentrated in volatile resource stocks and leans towards recent winners, which supports the concern raised by colleagues. SafeCore only reports its monthly holdings, so its daily returns are calculated by applying the monthly weights to the daily returns of the stocks it holds. The Capped SWIX is used as the benchmark throughout.

```{r PartB_Rets}
# SafeCore daily returns from its monthly holdings
SafeCore_Rets <- Q1_SafeCore_Returns(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks)

# Benchmark (J433) returns over the same dates
BM_Rets <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433", date >= min(SafeCore_Rets$date))
```

```{r Figure_SafeCore_Cum, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Cumulative returns: SafeCore vs Capped SWIX \\label{Figure_SafeCore_Cum}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# Cumulative returns of the fund and benchmark
g_cum <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, CP, color = Name)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Returns", subtitle = "SafeCore vs Capped SWIX (J433)", x = "Year", y = "Growth of R1") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cum)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_SafeCore_Cum} shows that SafeCore has outperformed its benchmark since 2015, ending the period well above the Capped SWIX.

```{r PartB_Monthly}
# Monthly returns for SafeCore and J433: chain daily returns into an index,
# keep the last trading day of each month, and take month-on-month returns
Monthly_Rets <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Yearmonth = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Yearmonth) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ret)) %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Ret)
```

```{r Table_Stats, results = 'asis'}
# Fund statistics relative to the benchmark (J433), over the last 3 and 5 years
Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  ) %>%
  mutate(Period = as.character(Period))

Table <- xtable(Tab_stats, caption = "SafeCore statistics relative to the Capped SWIX \\label{Table_Stats}", digits = 3)
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, include.rownames = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')
```

Table \ref{Table_Stats} compares SafeCore to the Capped SWIX over the last three and five years. These periods were chosen to focus on the fund's recent behaviour. SafeCore has outperformed over both periods, but with higher volatility than its benchmark.

The drawdown measures show how far the fund falls from a previous peak. Over five years, SafeCore's average drawdown is 9.8%, while that of the Capped SWIX is 6.9%, so when SafeCore falls, it tends to fall further. Its bear beta, which measures how the fund moves in months when the benchmark falls, is below one. This suggests that SafeCore is affected less by market declines in a normal down month but suffers larger declines when the market falls over a longer period.

SafeCore also has a higher adjusted Sharpe ratio over three years. The Sharpe ratio measures the return earned per unit of volatility. This means SafeCore has been rewarded for its risk, but it has still taken on more risk than its benchmark in recent years.

```{r Table_Downside, results = 'asis'}
# Downside risk measures for SafeCore and J433 (daily returns)
tabdownside <-
  table.DownsideRisk(left_join(SafeCore_Rets %>% select(date, SafeCore = Returns),
                               BM_Rets %>% select(date, J433 = Returns),
                               by = "date") %>% tbl_xts(.),
                     ci = 0.95, Rf = 0, MAR = 0)

# Keep semi deviation, downside deviation, maximum drawdown, VaR and ES
tabdownside <- tabdownside[c(1,5,7,8:11),]

Table <- xtable(tabdownside, caption = "Downside risk measures: SafeCore vs Capped SWIX \\label{Table_Downside}", digits = 4)
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')
```

The downside risk measures only consider losses, which is what matters most when volatility increases. Semi-deviation and downside deviation measure the volatility of returns below the mean and below zero. Value at Risk (VaR) is the loss that is exceeded on only 5% of days, and Expected Shortfall (ES) is the average loss on those worst days. Over the full period since 2015, SafeCore has lower downside risk than the Capped SWIX on every measure. For example, its maximum drawdown is 37.7%, while that of the Capped SWIX is 41.7%.

```{r Figure_Drawdown, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "SafeCore drawdown relative to the Capped SWIX \\label{Figure_Drawdown}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# Drawdown = percentage fall from the highest cumulative value reached so far.
# Difference = SafeCore drawdown minus J433 drawdown (positive = SafeCore fell less)
DD <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(date, Name, Drawdown) %>%
  spread(Name, Drawdown) %>%
  mutate(Diff = SafeCore - `Capped SWIX`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Diff))

g_dd <-
  DD %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(date, ymin = 0, ymax = Diff), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "SafeCore Drawdown Relative to the Capped SWIX",
       subtitle = "Above zero: SafeCore fell less than its benchmark",
       x = "Year", y = "Difference in drawdown") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The full-period result and the recent three and five year results point in different directions, so Figure \ref{Figure_Drawdown} looks at how this changed over time. It plots the difference between SafeCore's drawdown and that of the Capped SWIX, where positive values mean SafeCore fell less. SafeCore's advantage was mainly between 2015 and 2017 and in 2020. Since 2021, the difference has been close to zero or negative, especially in 2022. Therefore, SafeCore's protection on the downside has weakened in recent years, at the same time as offshore volatility has increased.

In summary, SafeCore has delivered strong returns, but the protection it offered in earlier years has weakened just as offshore volatility has increased. The next section therefore looks at where SafeCore’s risk comes from.

## Sources of SafeCore's volatility

```{r PartB_Risk}
# Share of SafeCore's volatility from each stock over the last 12 months
Risk_Contrib <- Q1_Risk_Contrib(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks, Months = 12)

# Sector of each stock, taken from the last month it was held
Sectors <-
  SafeCore %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Tickers, Sector)

# Total weight and total risk share per sector
Risk_Sector <-
  Risk_Contrib %>%
  left_join(Sectors, by = "Tickers") %>%
  # PAN and VAL have no sector in the SafeCore data but Index_Constituents lists both as Resources
  mutate(Sector = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("PAN", "VAL"), "Resources", Sector)) %>%
  group_by(Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = sum(wt), Risk = sum(Risk_Contrib)) %>%
  gather(Measure, Share, Weight, Risk)
```

```{r Figure_Risk, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "SafeCore weight and risk contribution by sector \\label{Figure_Risk}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
g_risk <-
  Risk_Sector %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Sector, Share, fill = Measure), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Where SafeCore's Volatility Comes From",
       subtitle = "Share of portfolio weight and share of volatility by sector",
       x = "", y = "Share") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_risk, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

To understand where SafeCore’s volatility comes from, Figure \ref{Figure_Risk} compares the share of the fund held in each sector to the share of the fund’s volatility that each sector is responsible for. This is based on the fund’s average holdings and daily returns over the last 12 months, which captures how the fund has been positioned over the past year. The risk contribution is not the same as the weight, as it also depends on how volatile each stock is and how closely it moves with the rest of the fund. A sector whose risk share is above its weight therefore adds more volatility than its size suggests.

The figure shows that SafeCore’s volatility is concentrated in resource stocks. Two holdings, Pan African Resources and Valterra Platinum, have no sector in the fund data and were classified as resources using the index constituent data. Resources make up just over a third of the fund but are responsible for around two thirds of its volatility, while financials and industrials add far less volatility than their weight. Resource stocks depend on global commodity prices, which makes them exposed to offshore shocks. Therefore, SafeCore’s risk comes mainly from the part of the fund that is most affected by the offshore volatility identified in Part A.

## Factor exposures

This section will construct a momentum and a low volatility score for each stock using price behaviour only. For momentum, each stock’s cumulative return over the past six months is calculated, excluding the most recent month. The most recent month is left out so that the score reflects a more persistent trend rather than the latest short-term movement. For low volatility, each stock’s realised volatility is calculated from the past six months of daily returns. A six month window captures recent price behaviour while being long enough not to react strongly to short-lived spikes. Since a lower volatility should correspond to a higher low volatility score, the sign of the volatility measure is reversed. Both measures are then standardised each month, so that every stock’s score is expressed relative to the other stocks at that point in time. This places the scores on the same scale as the third-party factor scores, which allows the two to be compared directly.

```{r PartB_Scores}
# Low volatility score
# Rolling SD of daily returns over 126 days (6 months) (same as Part A)
Own_LowVol <-
  Stocks %>%
  Q1_Rolling_Vol(Window = 126) %>%
  # Keep the last trading day of each month
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, LowVol = RollSD)

# Monthly stock returns (same steps as for SafeCore)
Stock_Monthly <-
  Stocks %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  # Cumulative index (missing returns set to zero)
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + coalesce(Returns, 0))) %>%
  # Keep the last trading day of each month
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  # Monthly return from the month-end index
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup()

# Momentum score
# 6 month rolling return (lagged one month to skip the latest month)
Own_Mom <-
  Stock_Monthly %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Mom = lag(RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Ret, n = 6, fill = NA, align = "right")) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, Mom)

# Combine both scores
Scores <-
  inner_join(Own_Mom, Own_LowVol, by = c("YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Mom), !is.na(LowVol)) %>%
  # Standardise each month (mean 0, SD 1)
  # Minus sign so that less volatile stocks get a higher score
  group_by(YM) %>%
  mutate(Own_Momentum = as.numeric(scale(Mom)),
         Own_LowVol = as.numeric(scale(-LowVol))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Add the third-party scores (one column per factor, matched by month)
  inner_join(Factor_Scores %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>% spread(Factor, Factor_Value),
             by = c("YM", "Tickers"))

```

```{r Figure_ScoreCor, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Correlation between own and third-party factor scores \\label{Figure_ScoreCor}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# Correlation across stocks each month between own and third-party scores
# Volatility Sensitivity is reversed so that a higher value means a less volatile stock
Score_Cor <-
  Scores %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(date = max(date),
            Momentum = cor(Own_Momentum, Momentum, use = "complete.obs"),
            `Low Volatility` = cor(Own_LowVol, `Volatility Sensitivity`, use = "complete.obs")) %>%
  select(-YM) %>%
  gather(Factor, Correlation, -date)

g_cor <-
  Score_Cor %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Correlation, color = Factor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Own vs Third-Party Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Monthly correlation across stocks", x = "Year", y = "Correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cor)
```

To compare the scores, Figure \ref{Figure_ScoreCor} shows the correlation between the own and third-party scores across all stocks in each month. The own momentum score is closely related to the third-party momentum score, with a correlation of between 0.6 and 0.85 in most months. The main exception is early 2021, when the correlation fell sharply. This suggests that the two scores measure different things. Therefore, the own low volatility score provides information that is not captured by the third-party scores.

The relationship between the own low volatility score and the third-party volatility sensitivity score is weaker. A higher volatility sensitivity score means a more volatile stock. This score was therefore reversed, which means that a higher value indicates a less volatile stock for both scores. Since late 2022, the correlation has been positive in most months. This means that the two scores mostly agree on which stocks are more volatile. However, the correlation is low and is negative in some periods. Therefore, the two scores do not measure exactly the same thing, and the own score adds information that the third-party scores do not capture.

```{r PartB_Composite}
# Latest month-end (shared by the holdings) constituents and factor scores
Last_Date <- max(SafeCore$date)

# Weights of SafeCore and the strategy indexes on that date
Weights <-
  bind_rows(
    SafeCore %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight = Weight) %>%
      mutate(Portfolio = "SafeCore"),
    Cons %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date, Index %in% c("Capped SWIX", "LowVol", "Momentum", "Value", "Quality")) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight, Portfolio = Index)
  )

# Composite score is the weighted sum of the stock scores in each portfolio
Composite <-
  Weights %>%
  left_join(Scores %>% filter(date == Last_Date), by = "Tickers") %>%
  group_by(Portfolio) %>%
  summarise(`Momentum (own)` = sum(weight * Own_Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Low volatility (own)` = sum(weight * Own_LowVol, na.rm = T),
            Momentum = sum(weight * Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Volatility Sensitivity` = sum(weight * `Volatility Sensitivity`, na.rm = T),
            Value = sum(weight * Value, na.rm = T),
            Growth = sum(weight * Growth, na.rm = T),
            `Earnings Quality` = sum(weight * `Earnings Quality`, na.rm = T)) %>%
  # Long format for plotting
  gather(Factor, Score, -Portfolio)
```

```{r Figure_Composite, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Composite factor scores: SafeCore, benchmark and strategy indexes \\label{Figure_Composite}", fig.height = 6, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
g_comp <-
  Composite %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Portfolio, Score, fill = Portfolio), stat = "identity") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Factor, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Composite Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Weighted average score of each portfolio's holdings (August 2026)",
       x = "Year", y = "Score") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_comp, x.vert = T)
```

To place SafeCore’s factor exposures in context, Figure \ref{Figure_Composite} shows the composite score of each portfolio, calculated as the weighted average score of its holdings in August 2026. All holdings had factor scores available, so the composite scores are based on the full portfolios. A positive score means the portfolio leans towards that factor, while a negative score means it leans away from it. As a check, each strategy index scores highest on its own factor, and the Capped SWIX sits close to zero on most factors. This is as expected for the broad market.

The figure shows that SafeCore has a strong momentum tilt, with a third-party momentum score as high as that of the Momentum index, while the Capped SWIX is close to zero. SafeCore also leans slightly towards value and earnings quality. However, it has no low volatility tilt, as its own low volatility score is slightly below that of its benchmark. Together with the results in Figure \ref{Figure_Risk}, this suggests that SafeCore holds stocks that have performed well recently (many of them resource stocks) without any defensive tilt to protect the fund when the market turns.

## Summary
In summary, SafeCore has outperformed its benchmark, but its protection during market declines has weakened as offshore volatility has increased. Its risk is concentrated in resource stocks, which are highly exposed to offshore shocks, and its factor exposures show a strong momentum tilt with no low volatility tilt. The team should be aware that SafeCore’s current positioning leaves it exposed to offshore shocks.

# Part C

## Dispersion

```{r PartC_Disp, cache = TRUE}
# Capped SWIX constituents (weight column is called weight)
J433_Cons <- Cons %>% filter(Index == "Capped SWIX")

# Benchmark returns
BM <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>% select(date, BM = Returns)

# Rolling 60 day (3 month) dispersion since 2020
m3_disp <- Dispersion_Prep(df_used = J433_Cons, BMUse = BM, BMSel = "weight", NSel = 60) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))
```

```{r Figure_Disp, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling dispersion of Capped SWIX constituents \\label{Figure_Disp}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
g_disp <-
  m3_disp %>%
  gather(Type, Value, starts_with("Dispersion")) %>%
  mutate(Type = ifelse(Type == "Dispersion_W", "Weighted", "Unweighted")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Type)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Sectional Volatility (Dispersion)",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (rolling 3 months)", x = "Year", y = "Dispersion") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_disp, y.pct = T)
```

Cross-sectional volatility (dispersion) measures the average weighted difference in returns between the constituents of an index and the parent index itself. When dispersion is low, the opportunity for active managers to differentiate their portfolios from the index is low, while high dispersion indicates a greater opportunity to do so. This section will calculate both weighted and unweighted dispersion for the Capped SWIX constituents over a rolling three month window. The weighted measure is used as the main measure, as SafeCore is managed against the Capped SWIX and the weighted measure compares each stock to the index return in line with its index weight. The unweighted measure is shown for comparison. The constituent data starts in August 2020, so the analysis covers the full period available since 2020.

Figure \ref{Figure_Disp} shows that dispersion is not constant, but increases sharply in certain periods before returning to lower levels. These periods of high dispersion represent the times when the opportunity to differentiate a portfolio from the Capped SWIX was greatest. The weighted measure is higher than the unweighted measure during most of these periods, which indicates that the largest constituents in particular moved apart from the index.

## Comovement between constituents

This section will look at how the comovement between the constituents of the Capped SWIX changes over time. The correlation coefficient measures the linear dependence between two assets, and asset market correlations typically increase in periods of turmoil, as turmoil leads to greater homogeneity in asset prices. For each month, the correlation matrix of the constituents’ daily returns is calculated and the average correlation across all pairs of stocks is taken.

```{r PartC_Cor}
Avg_Cor <- J433_Cons %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_split(YM) %>% map_df(~Q1_Month_Cor(.)) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))
```

```{r Figure_Cor, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Average correlation between Capped SWIX constituents \\label{Figure_Cor}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
g_avgcor <-
  Avg_Cor %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Avg_Cor), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Average Correlation Between Constituents",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (monthly)",
       x = "Year", y = "Average correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_avgcor)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_Cor} shows that the average correlation is generally low, but increases in certain periods (most notably in 2025 and 2026). Asset market correlations typically increase in periods of turmoil, as turmoil leads to asset market price homogeneity. It should be noted that a rolling correlation requires a look-back window and keeps the noise. A DCC estimate would instead provide a cleaner, noise-reduced version of the comovement structure between the constituents.

## Alpha opportunity and global uncertainty

This section will look at how the alpha opportunity has increased or decreased with key global macro factors. As the seminar focused on global policy uncertainty, the global economic policy uncertainty index is used. The months are stratified into environments, where months in which policy uncertainty is above its 85th percentile are classified as high uncertainty, months below its 25th percentile as low uncertainty, and the remaining months as other. The average weighted dispersion and average correlation are then compared across these environments.

```{r PartC_Enviro}
# Global economic policy uncertainty at month-end
EPU <- Uncertainty %>% filter(Ticker == "EPUCGLCP Index") %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, EPU = TRI)

# Month-end dispersion, monthly correlation and uncertainty in one data frame
df_comp_plot <-
left_join(
  m3_disp %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>% select(YM, Disp = Dispersion_W),
  Avg_Cor %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% select(YM, Cor = Avg_Cor),
  by = "YM"
) %>%
  left_join(EPU, by = "YM")
```

```{r Table_Enviro, results = 'asis'}
Enviro_Tab <-
  df_comp_plot %>% filter(!is.na(EPU), !is.na(Disp)) %>%
  mutate( hiEPU = quantile(EPU, 0.85),
          loEPU = quantile(EPU, 0.25)) %>%
  mutate(Enviro = ifelse(EPU > hiEPU, "High uncertainty",
                         ifelse(EPU < loEPU, "Low uncertainty",
                                "Other"))) %>%
  group_by(Enviro) %>% summarise(Dispersion = mean(Disp), Correlation = mean(Cor, na.rm = T))

Table <- xtable(Enviro_Tab, caption = "Average dispersion and correlation by level of global policy uncertainty \\label{Table_Enviro}", digits = 3)
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, include.rownames = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')
```

Table \ref{Table_Enviro} shows that both dispersion and correlation are higher in periods of high global policy uncertainty than in periods of low uncertainty. The higher correlation is consistent with turmoil leading to asset market price homogeneity. Since high dispersion means that the alpha opportunity (the ability to differentiate portfolios) is high, this suggests that the alpha opportunity in the local market has increased with global policy uncertainty. As only a small number of months fall into each environment, these results should be interpreted with caution.

## Summary

Overall, the results in Part C suggest that the alpha opportunity in the local market since 2020 has not been constant, but has risen in episodes. Dispersion between constituents rises sharply in certain periods, and these periods tend to coincide with high global policy uncertainty. Although stocks move together more closely during these periods, the larger spread in their returns suggests that active managers have had greater scope to differentiate their portfolios when global uncertainty is high.

# Conclusion

This report looked at how offshore uncertainty affects the local equity market and SafeCore. Part A showed that local volatility is not much higher than before, but is high in certain periods, mostly when offshore shocks occur. Part B showed that SafeCore has outperformed its benchmark, but its protection in down markets has weakened. Its volatility comes mainly from resource stocks, and it has a momentum tilt with no low volatility tilt. Part C showed that the alpha opportunity in the local market has been greater when global policy uncertainty is high. Therefore, SafeCore could benefit from more protection against volatility, while still making use of the opportunities that come with periods of high uncertainty.
